stem: What is the measure, in degrees, of angle $ACD$?
stimulus: A paleobotanist draws two parallel veins in a fossil leaf as lines $\ell$ and $m$. Point $A$ lies on line $\ell$. Points $B$ and $C$ lie on line $m$, with $B$ to the left of $C$. Point $P$ lies on line $\ell$ to the left of $A$, and point $D$ lies on line $m$ to the right of $C$. Line $\ell$ is parallel to line $m$. The measure of angle $PAB$ is $58^\circ$, and the measure of angle $BAC$ is $75^\circ$. Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
explanation: Angles $PAB$ and $ABC$ are alternate interior angles formed by the parallel lines and transversal $AB$, so angle $ABC$ is $58^\circ$. In triangle $ABC$, angle $ACB = 180 - 58 - 75 = 47^\circ$. Angle $ACD$ forms a linear pair with angle $ACB$, so it measures $180 - 47 = 133^\circ$. You can check this with the exterior angle rule: $58 + 75 = 133$.

A.why: You found the interior angle $ACB$ of the triangle and stopped. Angle $ACD$ is the exterior angle beside it, so you still need to subtract from 180.

B.why: This is angle $ABC$, the alternate interior partner of angle $PAB$. It is at vertex $B$, not at vertex $C$, where the question asks.

C.why: You found the exterior angle at $B$ ($180 - 58$) when the question asks for the exterior angle at $C$.

stem: What is the measure, in degrees, of angle $CDE$?
stimulus: A nutrition scientist sketches a divided-plate diagram in which segments $AD$ and $BE$ intersect at point $C$, forming triangles $ABC$ and $DEC$. The measure of angle $CAB$ is $64^\circ$ and the measure of angle $ABC$ is $51^\circ$. In triangle $DEC$, the measure of angle $CDE$ is $x^\circ$ and the measure of angle $CED$ is $(3x - 5)^\circ$. Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
explanation: In triangle $ABC$, angle $ACB = 180 - 64 - 51 = 65^\circ$. Angles $ACB$ and $DCE$ are vertical angles, so angle $DCE$ is also $65^\circ$. In triangle $DEC$, $x + (3x - 5) + 65 = 180$, so $4x = 120$ and $x = 30$. Angle $CDE$ measures $30^\circ$.

B.why: This is angle $ACB$, which is equal to its vertical angle $DCE$. It is the link between the two triangles, but it is not angle $CDE$.

C.why: This is angle $CED$, which equals $3(30) - 5$. You solved for $x$ correctly but then evaluated the expression for the wrong angle.

D.why: This is $180 - 65$, the combined measure of angles $CDE$ and $CED$. You still need to split that total between the two angles.

stem: What is the measure, in degrees, of angle $ACB$?
stimulus: A printmaker carves a linoleum block in the shape of quadrilateral $ABCD$, in which side $AB$ is parallel to side $DC$. A cut along diagonal $AC$ divides the block into two triangles. The measure of angle $ADC$ is $71^\circ$, the measure of angle $DAC$ is $47^\circ$, and the measure of angle $ABC$ is $96^\circ$. Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
explanation: In triangle $ADC$, angle $ACD = 180 - 71 - 47 = 62^\circ$. Because $AB \parallel DC$ and $AC$ is a transversal, angle $BAC$ is the alternate interior angle to angle $ACD$, so it is also $62^\circ$. In triangle $ABC$, angle $ACB = 180 - 96 - 62 = 22^\circ$.

A.why: You assumed the trapezoid is isosceles, which made angle $BCD$ equal to angle $ADC$ ($71^\circ$), and then subtracted 62. The question never says the legs are equal.

C.why: This is angle $ACD$, which is equal to angle $BAC$. It is the value you carry across the parallel sides, not the angle the question asks for.

D.why: This is the whole angle $BCD$ ($180 - 96$). Angle $ACB$ is only the part of it on the far side of the diagonal.

stem: What is the measure, in degrees, of angle $ADC$?
stimulus: A musicologist diagrams the frame of a percussion triangle as triangle $ABC$, in which $AB = AC$. Line $\ell$ passes through $A$ and is parallel to $BC$. Point $P$ lies on line $\ell$ on the same side of $A$ as $B$, and the measure of angle $PAB$ is $70^\circ$. Point $D$ lies on side $BC$ between $B$ and $C$ so that the measure of angle $BAD$ is $25^\circ$. Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
explanation: Because $\ell \parallel BC$, angle $ABC$ is the alternate interior angle to angle $PAB$, so it is $70^\circ$. Since $AB = AC$, angle $ACB$ is also $70^\circ$ and angle $BAC = 40^\circ$. Angle $ADC$ is an exterior angle of triangle $ABD$, so it equals $70 + 25 = 95^\circ$. You can check this in triangle $ADC$: $95 + 70 + 15 = 180$.

A.why: This is angle $DAC$ ($40 - 25$), a different angle in the same triangle as angle $ADC$.

B.why: This is the base angle at $B$ (and at $C$) that you get from the parallel lines. It is a step toward angle $ADC$, not the answer.

C.why: This is angle $ADB$, the interior angle of triangle $ABD$ at $D$. Angle $ADC$ is its supplement, the exterior angle beside it.

stem: What is the measure, in degrees, of angle $PBT$?
stimulus: An immunologist sketches a bent antibody arm as a path between two parallel guide lines. Line $\ell$ is parallel to line $m$, and $\ell$ is above $m$. Point $A$ lies on $\ell$ and point $B$ lies on $m$. Point $P$ lies between the two lines, to the right of both $A$ and $B$, and segments $AP$ and $PB$ are drawn. Point $R$ lies on $\ell$ to the right of $A$, point $S$ lies on $m$ to the right of $B$, and point $T$ lies on $m$ to the left of $B$. The measure of angle $RAP$ is $(2x)^\circ$, the measure of angle $SBP$ is $(3x - 8)^\circ$, and the measure of angle $APB$ is $107^\circ$. Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
explanation: Draw a line through $P$ parallel to $\ell$ and $m$. It splits angle $APB$ into two angles that are alternate interior angles to angles $RAP$ and $SBP$, so $2x + (3x - 8) = 107$. Then $5x = 115$ and $x = 23$, which makes angle $SBP = 3(23) - 8 = 61^\circ$. Angle $PBT$ forms a linear pair with angle $SBP$, so it measures $180 - 61 = 119^\circ$.

A.why: This is the value of $x$, not an angle measure. You still have to substitute it into the expression and finish the chain.

B.why: This is angle $SBP$, the acute angle on the right of $B$. Angle $PBT$ is on the other side of $B$ and is supplementary to it.

D.why: This is $180 - 46$, the obtuse angle segment $AP$ makes with line $\ell$ at $A$. The question asks about the angle at $B$.

stem: What is the measure, in degrees, of angle $AED$?
stimulus: An urban planner maps two parallel avenues as lines $\ell$ and $m$. Street $p$ crosses $\ell$ at point $A$ and $m$ at point $B$. Street $q$ crosses $\ell$ at point $C$ and $m$ at point $D$. Points $A$ and $D$ are on the left and points $C$ and $B$ are on the right, and the two streets intersect at point $E$ between the avenues. The measure of angle $CAE$ is $63^\circ$. Street $q$ makes an angle of $128^\circ$ with avenue $m$ at $D$, measured from ray $DC$ to the part of $m$ that extends to the left of $D$, away from $B$. Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
explanation: The $128^\circ$ angle forms a linear pair with angle $EDB$, so angle $EDB = 52^\circ$. Because $\ell \parallel m$ and street $p$ is a transversal, angle $EBD$ is the alternate interior angle to angle $CAE$, so it is $63^\circ$. In triangle $BED$, angle $BED = 180 - 63 - 52 = 65^\circ$. Points $A$, $E$, and $B$ are on one line, so angle $AED = 180 - 65 = 115^\circ$.

A.why: This is angle $EDB$, the supplement of the given $128^\circ$. It is the first link in the chain, not the angle at $E$.

B.why: This is angle $BED$, the interior angle of the triangle at $E$, which also equals its vertical angle $AEC$. Angle $AED$ is the angle supplementary to it.

D.why: This is $180 - 63$, the obtuse angle street $p$ makes with avenue $\ell$ at $A$. It is at the wrong vertex.

stem: What is the measure, in degrees, of angle $PSR$?
stimulus: A meteorologist outlines a wedge of cold air on a weather map as triangle $PQR$. Point $S$ lies on side $QR$ between $Q$ and $R$, and segment $PS$ is drawn so that $QS = PS$. The measure of angle $QPR$ is $94^\circ$, and the measure of angle $PRQ$ is $44^\circ$. Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
explanation: In triangle $PQR$, angle $PQR = 180 - 94 - 44 = 42^\circ$. Since $QS = PS$, triangle $PQS$ is isosceles with equal base angles, so angle $QPS$ is also $42^\circ$. Angle $PSR$ is an exterior angle of triangle $PQS$, so it equals $42 + 42 = 84^\circ$. You can check this in triangle $PSR$: $84 + 52 + 44 = 180$.

A.why: This is angle $PQR$, which is also equal to base angle $QPS$. It is a step in the chain, not the angle at $S$.

C.why: You assumed $PS$ bisects angle $QPR$, which gives $47 + 42$. The question never says that. The given condition is $QS = PS$.

D.why: This is angle $PSQ$, the interior angle of triangle $PQS$ at $S$. Angle $PSR$ is the supplementary angle on the other side of $PS$.

stem: What is the measure, in degrees, of angle $ACD$?
stimulus: An ornithologist models a flight path with triangle $ABC$. Point $A$ lies on line $\ell$, and points $B$ and $C$ lie on line $m$, with $B$ to the left of $C$. Line $\ell$ is parallel to line $m$. Point $P$ lies on $\ell$ to the left of $A$, point $Q$ lies on $\ell$ to the right of $A$, and point $D$ lies on $m$ to the right of $C$. The measure of angle $PAB$ is $(4x)^\circ$, the measure of angle $BAC$ is $(2x)^\circ$, and the measure of angle $CAQ$ is $(3x + 5)^\circ$. Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
explanation: The three angles at $A$ lie along line $\ell$, so $4x + 2x + (3x + 5) = 180$. Then $9x = 175$ and $x = \frac{175}{9}$. Angle $ACB$ is the alternate interior angle to angle $CAQ$, so it measures $3\left(\frac{175}{9}\right) + 5 = \frac{190}{3}$ degrees. Angle $ACD$ forms a linear pair with angle $ACB$, so it measures $180 - \frac{190}{3} = \frac{350}{3}$ degrees.

A.why: This is the value of $x$, not an angle measure. You stopped before substituting it into any angle.

B.why: This is angle $ACB$, the interior angle of the triangle at $C$. Angle $ACD$ is the exterior angle beside it, so you still need to subtract from 180.

C.why: This is $4x$, which is angle $PAB$ and also its alternate interior partner, angle $ABC$. It is at vertex $B$, not at $C$.
